tagline: Pines above the Verde Valley, mining streets on Cleopatra Hill
intro: SR 89A traverses the Prescott National Forest at Mingus Mountain in Arizona’s Black Hills. Forest Service roads branch from the highway toward the summit, where views include the Verde Valley and Sycamore Canyon Wilderness. The Forest Service describes a pine setting with hiking, camping, hang gliding and paragliding.

Jerome’s mining industry built its own transport connections: United Verde constructed wagon roads to Prescott, the Verde Valley and the railroad depot at Ash Fork. Wagon transport proved expensive, and the company stopped operations in late 1884 after copper prices fell. William A. Clark bought the properties four years later and ordered a narrow-gauge railway to Jerome Junction.

Coming from the Prescott side, the mountain excursion branches off SR 89A before the journey reaches Jerome. Woodchute Wilderness lies north of the highway’s highest point. Jerome occupies Cleopatra Hill above the Verde Valley, its surviving buildings set along winding roads on the steep mountainside.

moments.title: Mingus Mountain
moments.text: A 60-foot steel fire tower stands atop Mingus Mountain, replacing a shorter wooden tower in 1935. Its wooden cab has an overhanging front porch and a gabled roof. The lookout complex entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1988. Forest Service roads reach the summit from SR 89A. The mountain offers views of the Verde Valley and Sycamore Canyon Wilderness; the surrounding recreation area includes a small lake periodically stocked with rainbow trout. Hang gliding and paragliding are among the Forest Service’s listed activities here, alongside hiking, horseback riding and mountain biking in the pines.

moments.title: Jerome
moments.text: Jerome’s buildings follow winding streets on a steep mountainside above the Verde Valley. The copper mines supported more than 10,000 residents in the 1920s, but the population fell below 100 after mining ended in 1953. The town also endured ground subsidence: dozens of buildings, including the post office and jail, were lost as the ground sank during the 1930s. In 1953, residents organized the Jerome Historical Society and opened a museum. In 1956, the society completed negotiations with Phelps Dodge to prevent further demolition in the town’s main area. Houses, commercial buildings and civic buildings survive within the historic district.

moments.title: Sliding Jail
moments.text: Jerome’s third jail began as part of a larger wood-and-tin structure, built in 1905. In 1938, it began moving downhill after dynamite blasting changed the mountainside. The jail tore free of the original building and ended up on Hull Avenue. Residents changed the road to pass it; Arizona’s transportation department later moved the jail to its present position. The Jerome Historical Society took control in 2017 and stabilized the remaining walls. Earth movement left the structure unusable but did not destroy it completely. An iron fence surrounds the surviving jail, whose walls were stabilized.
